note: System One Security Judges (arXiv 2609.33401v3, 3 Oct 2026, the current version on 2026-10-12). The director's treatment was written from v1 (27 Sep 2026); the producer moved the receipts and the wording of l04, l07, l10 and l13 to v3 because v3 rewords the v1 abstract finding and drops the v1 sentence 'Confidently allowed attacks never reach the second judge'. The four on-screen figures (0.2%, 9%, 1%, 7%) are the same after rounding in v1 and v3. One model (Jev) on one task (WAInjectBench-text, prompt injection, test split) carries every number. All results are the author's offline runs on public benchmarks. Page numbers are v3 PDF pages. Every other digit on screen is a source tag (section, page) or the arXiv id.

numbers.0.2: 0.2%: Jev's mean unsafe probability over the 1,446 WAInjectBench test inputs it scored below 0.1 (1,446 of 1,612 test inputs, so 'most inputs'). Paper value 0.205%. An average, measured, author's runs, one model on one benchmark (sec 5.2, p. 12; v1 sec 5.2, p. 13: 0.205% over 1,444 inputs). The line says 'average' and 'about'.
numbers.9: 9%: the share of those same 1,446 low-score inputs labelled unsafe: 133 of 1,446, 9.20% (sec 5.2, p. 12; v1: 9.14%). Measured. The line says 'about'.
numbers.1: Two uses. (a) 1%: the miss limit, epsilon = 0.01, a SETTING chosen by the author (the strictest of 1, 5 and 10%), not a result: thresholds were picked on selection inputs so that at most 1% of unsafe selection inputs are allowed (and at most 5% of benign ones blocked), then held fixed for confirmation and test (sec 6.2, p. 17; 'the 1% selection miss limit', sec 6.3 and Table 13). On screen it carries the label 'a setting, not a result'. (b) page 1 in the source tag of the abstract receipt.
numbers.7: 7%: Jev's automatic coverage on WAInjectBench test with independent (separate) allow and block thresholds at the 1% selection miss limit, original scores: 6.70%, 108 blocks and 0 allows, tau_L = 0.000, tau_H = 0.525, passes the confirmation and test checks (sec 6.4, p. 19; Table 14, p. 20). Absolute share of test inputs, measured. The separate-threshold analysis is one of the three the paper calls exploratory (sec 8, p. 24). The line says 'about'.
numbers.4.2: section 4.2, Classification Results and Error Patterns (p. 7): source tag for 'missed every attack of that kind'
numbers.5.2: section 5.2, Calibration and High-Confidence Errors (p. 12): source tag
numbers.6.5: section 6.5, Confidence Ranking and Identical Scores (p. 21): receipt label
numbers.6.6: section 6.6, Language-Model Judges as Potential Reviewers (p. 21 to 22): receipt label
numbers.2609.33401: arXiv id (p. 1), used in the end card credit

evidence_incidental.2: abstract crop (p. 1): a grey sliver of the vertical arXiv identifier stamp ('arXiv:2609.33401v3') at the crop's left edge; the text extractor reads one glyph of it as '2'. Not a figure and not legible on screen.

claims.l01: A question, not a claim. The paper's own question (sec 1, p. 2): 'When can developers use System One model judgments and probabilities to automate security checks in agentic software?' The drawing shows a judge stamping SAFE on an input card; the attack mark revealed on 'trust' stands for attack-derived text classified as safe, which the paper reports (sec 4.2, sec 5.2).
claims.l02: Sec 1 (p. 1 to 2) and sec 2.1 (p. 3): System One models take an input and a developer-defined question and assign probabilities to predefined answers such as safe or unsafe; the paper evaluates them as security checks for agents on three tasks: prompt-injection detection (WAInjectBench), interaction risk (R-Judge) and harmful requests (AgentHarm) (Table 1, p. 5).
claims.l03: Sec 1 (p. 1 to 2) and eq. 1 (sec 6.1, p. 17): a security policy converts the unsafe probability into allow (below tau_L), block (above tau_H) or escalate for review (in between). The rail pins are schematic; no threshold value is shown (the 10.5% and 89.5% of Fig. 3 are left out).
claims.l04: Calibration definition: sec 1 (p. 2) 'the agreement between reported probabilities and observed outcomes', and sec 5 (p. 10). Second sentence: abstract finding (1), p. 1, v3: 'High overall accuracy and low average calibration error can conceal attacks classified as safe with high confidence within particular groups' (receipt crop). The intro jar is tagged 'example' and carries no number.
claims.l05: Sec 5.2 (p. 12): Jev assigns unsafe probabilities below 0.1 to 1,446 of 1,612 WAInjectBench test inputs; their mean predicted probability is 0.205%. 'Most inputs' = 1,446 of 1,612 (Table 2 test size, p. 5). One model, one benchmark. The model name Jev appears only as a small tag.
claims.l06: Sec 5.2 (p. 12): of those 1,446 inputs, 133 (9.20%) are unsafe. In WAInjectBench unsafe inputs are attack-derived text segments (sec 3.2, p. 4), so 'attacks'. The jar draws 9 of 100 marbles amber from _observed.
claims.l07: Sec 5.2 (p. 12): 'Of these 133 unsafe inputs, 130 lack direct attack instructions (no-EI)', so 'nearly all'. Sec 4.2 (p. 7): 'Jev misses all 130 unsafe no-EI inputs while falsely flagging just one benign input' (test split). The EI/no-EI analysis is one the paper calls exploratory (sec 8, p. 24); the on-screen tag says so.
claims.l08: Sec 6.5 (p. 21): 'Jev assigns p_i = 0 to 1,320 shared WAInjectBench inputs, including 102 misses'. The other 1,218 zero-score inputs are correct safe predictions, i.e. benign inputs, so 'many benign inputs'. Zero is the lowest possible unsafe probability. The bucket draws amber cores at _tieMiss/_tieAll (about 8%); no count is shown.
claims.l09: Sec 6.5 (p. 21), verbatim bold run-in (receipt crop): 'Thresholds cannot separate correct and incorrect decisions with the same score.' Same paragraph: 'Any positive allow threshold admits all zero-score inputs, including the missed attacks.' The drawing tips the whole bucket through the allow gate when the pin moves right, and keeps it all out when the pin moves back.
claims.l10: First sentence: sec 6.6 (p. 22), receipt crop: 'Reviewing only uncertain inputs leaves confident mistakes unreviewed, even when another judge could detect them.' Also p. 21: 'A judge can correct the first model's missed attack only when the review rule forwards that input.' Second sentence: sec 6.6 (p. 21): 'Among misses with max(p_i, 1 - p_i) >= 0.95, each judge detects at most five of Jev's 130 misses', so 'only a few'. This compares seven language-model judges with Jev on the same WAInjectBench test inputs ('a separate test'); the paper calls the cross-model error analysis exploratory (sec 8, p. 24). The tray drawing flips cards at _fixed/_confident (5 of 130, about 1 in 26), rounded down for the drawing; no count is shown. The drawing is a generic review rule, not the 1% policy.
claims.l11: Sec 6.2 (p. 17) and sec 6.3, Table 13 (p. 17 to 18): with symmetric thresholds chosen at the 1% selection miss limit (and the 5% benign-block limit), Jev's WAInjectBench test coverage is 0.00%: every test input is sent for review. Primary protocol. The line speaks about this model only (Decider, GPT-4.1 and Qwen3-8B did the same). The 1% is labelled on screen as a setting, not a result.
claims.l12: Sec 6.4 (p. 19) and Table 14 (p. 20): with independent allow and block thresholds at the same limit, Jev's WAInjectBench coverage rises from zero to 6.70%, 'entirely through 108 blocks'; Allowed 0, tau_L = 0.000, passes confirmation and test. Exploratory per sec 8 (on-screen tag). Visual only, no words: the zero-score bucket slides past the closed allow gate into review. That follows from tau_L = 0.000 in Table 14 and eq. 1 (sec 6.1, p. 17: inputs exactly at a threshold escalate), and sec 6.5 (p. 21: a positive allow threshold would admit the whole zero-score group).
claims.l13: Sec 8, External validity (p. 24): the benchmarks are public (sec 3.2) and text-only (WAInjectBench-text, R-Judge records, AgentHarm requests); 'Results may differ for adaptive attacks, other languages, and multimodal inputs.' Also 'Public benchmarks may overlap training data'.
claims.l14: Sec 1 (p. 2): 'Developers therefore need to validate labels, probabilities, and the actions chosen by the policy together'; sec 9 (p. 24 to 25). The closing words repeat the hook. End card: handle, paper title, arXiv id, 'unofficial explainer'.
